title: My work and my week
cando: describe your job, your week and what you have to do

about.text: In this lesson you talk about your job, your week and what you have to do. You meet a new colleague, and you read a job advert and part of a contract. Then you ask the right questions about a new job before you say yes.
goals: Say what your job is like and what you do in a usual week.
Say what you are doing this week: I'm working on a new project.
Say what you have to do, and what you don't have to do.
Read a job advert and part of a contract, and describe a job in three parts.
Ask what a new job needs before you accept it.

chapters.title: A new colleague
chapters.text:
In this lesson you talk about your work and your week.
First, you listen to Amina. It is her first day in a new job. Her colleague Tomasz welcomes her.
Amina asks: What's the job like? Tomasz says: It's busy, but it's never boring.
Then she asks: What do I have to do?
Listen to have to. We say it fast, like one word. The v in have sounds like f.

chapters.title: Every week, this week, and have to
chapters.text:
There are two grammar points in this lesson.
One. For every day and every week, say: I work, she starts. We answer calls from customers all day.
For now, or for this week only, use am, is or are and -ing. This week I'm working on a new project.
Two. Have to means there is no choice. I have to start at eight. She has to wear a uniform.
Don't have to means it is not necessary. You don't have to wear a suit. It is your choice.
Need to is like have to. I need to finish this report today.

chapters.title: A job advert and a contract
chapters.text:
Next, you read a job advert and part of a contract.
The advert is short. It says the hours, the pay and what you need for the job.
Read one line carefully: No experience needed. That means you don't have to have experience. It is good news. You can apply!
Then you describe a job in three parts. What do you do? What do you have to do? And what is it like?

chapters.title: Before you say yes
chapters.text:
In the task, a new colleague asks about your job. Tell her what you do, what you have to do and what the job is like.
Then a manager offers you a new job. Before you accept, ask questions.
Do I have to work at weekends? Is there any overtime? Is it full-time or part-time?
Ask before you sign the contract, not after.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a story or an article about work.
Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again and answer the questions.

warmup.prompt: A new colleague asks: What's your job like? What do you say first?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. People often answer in two parts: one word, then a little more. It's busy, but I like my team.

conversation.title: A new colleague
conversation.setting: It is Monday morning at Greenway Travel. Amina starts her new job in customer service today. Tomasz works in the same department.
lines: Tomasz
Hi, you're Amina, right? I'm Tomasz. Welcome to the department!
Amina
Thanks! It's my first day. So, what's the job like?
Tomasz
It's busy, but it's never boring. We answer calls from customers all day.
Amina
What do I have to do in the morning?
Tomasz
You have to start at eight. First, you check the emails and prepare a list of tasks.
Amina
OK. Do I have to wear a uniform?
Tomasz
No, you don't have to. But you have to wear your staff card.
Amina
Right. And what are you working on at the moment?
Tomasz
This week I'm helping our manager with a new project. The deadline is Friday, so it's a bit stressful.
Amina
Oh dear. Do I need to attend any training?
Tomasz
Yes. Everyone in the department has to attend the training on Wednesday. It's long and quite tiring.
Amina
OK. I need to organise my week, then.
Tomasz
Good idea. And don't worry. Everyone here is very friendly.

questions.q: What time does Amina have to start?
questions.why: Tomasz says: You have to start at eight.

questions.q: Does Amina have to wear a uniform?
questions.a: No, but she has to wear her staff card.
questions.why: Tomasz says: No, you don't have to. But you have to wear your staff card.

questions.q: Why is Tomasz's week a bit stressful?
questions.a: The project has a deadline on Friday.
wrong: He has a lot of new customers.
questions.why: Tomasz says: The deadline is Friday, so it's a bit stressful.

phrases.use: Describing a job in two parts.

Saying the last day to finish a piece of work.

items.meaning: All the people who work for a company or in one place.
items.example: All new staff have to attend the training.

items.meaning: The person who plans the work of a team and tells them what to do.
items.example: My manager makes the shift list on Friday.

items.meaning: A person who buys something from a shop or a company.
items.example: We answer calls from customers all day.

items.meaning: One piece of work that you have to do.
items.example: My first task every morning is to check the emails.

items.meaning: A big piece of work with a plan and an end date. Often a team does it together.
items.example: I'm working on a new project with two colleagues.

items.meaning: The last day or time to finish a piece of work.
items.example: The deadline for the report is Friday at five.

items.meaning: One part of a big company or a hospital. Each part does one kind of work.
items.example: Priya works in the sales department.

items.meaning: Lessons that show you how to do your job, or how to use something new.
items.example: The training for new staff is on Wednesday.

items.meaning: To go to a meeting, a class or a training day.
items.example: Everyone has to attend the meeting on Monday.

items.meaning: To plan things and put them in order, so the work is easy.
items.example: I organise my tasks every Monday morning.

items.meaning: To get something ready before it starts, or before you need it.
items.example: I prepare the meeting room before the manager arrives.

items.meaning: To get money for the work you do.
items.example: I earn more money when I work at the weekend.

items.meaning: Making you feel worried, because there is too much to do or not much time.
items.example: The week before a deadline is always stressful.

items.meaning: Making you want to rest or sleep.
items.example: The late shift is long and tiring.

sound.title: have to
sound.explain: Say have to fast, like one word. The v in have sounds like f: haf-to. In has to, the s sounds like the s in bus. To is short and quiet. Listen, then say each group.
groups: I have to · you have to · we have to
she has to · he has to · everyone has to
I don't have to · she doesn't have to
lines: You have to start at eight.
Everyone has to attend the training.
No, you don't have to.

sayIt.instructions: Say Amina's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Does have to sound quick, like one word?
lines: Thanks! It's my first day. So, what's the job like?
What do I have to do in the morning?
OK. Do I have to wear a uniform?
Oh dear. Do I need to attend any training?

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. The first two talk about time in two different ways. The last three talk about rules at work.
examples: We answer calls from customers all day.
This week I'm helping our manager with a new project.
You have to start at eight.
Everyone in the department has to attend the training on Wednesday.
spot.question: Which sentence is about every day, and which is about this week only? Which sentences mean there is no choice? Which one means it is not necessary?
spot.answer: Every day: we answer calls. This week only: I'm helping, with am + -ing. No choice: you have to, everyone has to. Not necessary: you don't have to. It is your choice.

rules.title: Every week, or this week only: I work, I'm working
rule: Every day or every week: I work in sales. She starts at eight.
Now, or for a short time: This week I'm working on a new project.
Words for every week: usually, always, every day, on Mondays.
Words for now: now, today, this week, at the moment.
Some verbs don't usually take -ing: know, like, want, need. Say: I know. Not: I'm knowing.
rules.mistake: Not: Usually I'm starting at eight. Say: I usually start at eight.

rules.title: have to, don't have to, need to
rule: have to + a verb: there is no choice. I have to start at eight.
He, she and it: has to. She has to wear a uniform.
don't have to: it is not necessary, but you can. You don't have to wear a suit.
Questions: Do I have to work on Saturdays? Does he have to drive?
need to is like have to: I need to finish this today.
rules.mistake: Not: She have to work late. Not: I have to working. Say: She has to work late.

practice.q: I usually ___ work at eight o'clock.
practice.why: Usually is about every day, so say start.

practice.q: Carlos is busy. He ___ on a new project at the moment.
practice.why: At the moment is about now: is + -ing.

practice.q: She ___ wear a uniform at work. It's a rule.
practice.why: She, he and it take has to.

practice.q: You ___ bring lunch. Lunch is free in the staff café.
practice.why: The café is free, so it is not necessary.

practice.q: ___ I have to work on Saturdays?
practice.why: A question with I: Do I have to …?

practice.q: He doesn't ___ to start early on Fridays.
practice.why: After doesn't, say have, not has.

practice.q: I need ___ finish this report today.
practice.why: need to + a verb: I need to finish.
Know doesn't usually take -ing: he knows.

practice.q: Our office ___ at half past eight every day.
practice.why: Every day: it opens, with s.

practice.q: It's a busy week, so I ___ stay late tonight.
practice.why: It is a busy week, so it is necessary: I need to.

yourTurn.prompt: Write about your week. Say what you usually do, one thing that is different this week, and two things you have to do. It can be real or made up.
yourTurn.model: I usually work from nine to five in a hotel. This week I'm working late, because a colleague is on holiday. I have to check every room before the guests arrive. On Thursday I have to attend a training day. I don't have to work at the weekend, so I can rest.

text.title: A job advert and part of a contract
text.body:
PRACTICE ADVERT: this company does not exist.

OFFICE ASSISTANT
Greenway Travel, Kellbridge

Part-time: 25 hours a week, Monday to Friday
Salary: £15,860 a year
Full-time work is possible after one year.

THE JOB
Answer calls and emails from customers.
Organise meetings for the sales team.
Prepare letters and simple reports.

YOU NEED
Good computer skills.
No experience needed. We give full training.
You don't have to speak another language, but it helps.

Apply online by 30 September.

- - - - - - - -

PRACTICE CONTRACT: part of a contract, for practice only.

CONTRACT OF EMPLOYMENT (PART)
Employer: Greenway Travel
Employee: Omar Hassan

3. HOURS
Normal hours: 9.30 am to 2.30 pm, Monday to Friday.
The employer can ask you to work up to 5 hours of overtime a week.
Overtime pay: £12.20 an hour.

4. HOLIDAY
20 days a year. You can't take holiday in December.

5. THE FIRST 3 MONTHS
In your first 3 months, you or the employer can end this contract. You only have to tell the other one a week before.

gist.a: a part-time job in an office
wrong: a full-time job in a shop
gist.why: The advert says: Office assistant. Part-time: 25 hours a week.

gist.a: part of Omar's contract for the job
gist.why: It says: Contract of employment (part). Employee: Omar Hassan.

detail.q: Do you need experience for this job?
detail.why: The advert says: No experience needed. We give full training.

detail.q: Lena speaks only English. Can she apply?
detail.a: Yes. She doesn't have to speak another language.
wrong: No. She has to speak two languages.
detail.why: The advert says: You don't have to speak another language. It is not necessary.

detail.q: How much overtime can the employer ask for?
detail.why: The contract says: up to 5 hours of overtime a week.

detail.q: Omar wants a holiday in December. What does the contract say?
detail.a: He can't take holiday in December.
wrong: He can take 20 days in December.
He has to ask the customers.
detail.why: The contract says: You can't take holiday in December.

items.meaning: A short text in a newspaper or online. It tells people about a job, or about something to buy.
items.example: I saw an advert for a job at the hospital.

items.meaning: A paper that you and a company both sign. It says the work, the hours and the pay.
items.example: Read the contract carefully before you sign it.

items.meaning: The money you get for a year's work. The company pays it every month.
items.example: The salary is £22,000 a year.

items.meaning: Extra hours of work, after your normal hours.
items.example: I did three hours of overtime last week.

items.meaning: The work you did before, and what you learned from it.
items.example: I've got two years' experience in a shop.

items.meaning: Something you can do well, because you learned it or practised it.
items.example: Good computer skills are important for this job.

items.meaning: To ask for a job or a place on a course, often online.
items.example: I want to apply for the office job.

items.meaning: The company or person that pays you to work.
items.example: My employer pays for my training.

items.meaning: A person who works for a company and gets money from it.
items.example: The company has forty employees.

items.meaning: Working all the normal hours of a week, often 35 to 40 hours.
items.example: She has a full-time job in a bank.

items.meaning: Working only some of the hours of a week, for example mornings only.
items.example: I work part-time, so I can study in the afternoons.

model.title: A job in three parts
model.body:
What I do: I work in a big supermarket. I fill the shelves, and I help customers find things. On busy days I work on the tills.
What I have to do: I have to start at six in the morning. I have to be careful with the heavy boxes. I don't have to wear a suit, but I have to wear a uniform.
What it's like: It's quite tiring, but my team is great. This month I'm training two new employees, and I enjoy it.

write.task: Describe a job in three parts. It can be your job, a job you did before, or a job you want. Use the three headings in the model, and write two or three sentences for each part.
checklist: I wrote three parts: what I do, what I have to do, and what it's like.
I used have to or don't have to at least twice.
I wrote one sentence about this week or this month with I'm + -ing.
I used two words from this lesson, like tiring, customer or deadline.

card.title: Before you say yes
card.situation: Your new colleague Lena asks about your job. Later, Priya from Greenway Travel phones you. She wants to give you a part-time job as an office assistant.
card.goal: Tell Lena what you do, what you have to do and what the job is like. Then ask Priya four questions before you accept the new job.

phrases: I have to … . I don't have to …
It's busy, but it's never boring.
Before I accept, can I ask some questions?
Do I have to work at weekends?
Is there any overtime? Do I need to attend any training?
prepare.notes: Make notes in three parts: what you do, what you have to do, and what your job is like. Then write four questions for the new job: the hours, weekends, overtime and training.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, tell your teacher about your job. Then your teacher is Priya, a manager at a new company. Ask your four questions before you accept the job.
doIt.wehel: You are Priya, a manager at Greenway Travel. You phone me to offer me a part-time job as an office assistant. I have some questions before I accept. Answer my questions about the hours, weekends, overtime and training. Then ask me about my job now. Use simple English.

model.title: The phone call
lines: Priya
Hello, it's Priya from Greenway Travel. I'd like to offer you the job!
You
Thank you! That's great news. Before I accept, can I ask some questions?
Priya
Of course.
You
Do I have to work at weekends?
Priya
No, you don't have to. The office is closed at weekends.
You
Good. Is there any overtime?
Priya
Sometimes, before a big deadline. We pay £12.20 an hour for it.
You
And do I need to attend any training?
Priya
Yes. All new staff have to do two days of training in the first week.
You
OK. And is it full-time or part-time?
Priya
It's part-time, 25 hours a week. So, what do you do at the moment?
You
I work in a café. I usually start at seven. This month I'm working on Saturdays too.
Priya
Great. So, do you accept the job?
You
Yes, I do. Thank you very much!
compare: Did you say what you do, what you have to do and what the job is like?
Did you ask your questions before you accepted?
Did you ask about weekends, overtime and training?
Did you use I usually … for every week, and I'm … -ing for this week?

canDo: I can say what my job is like and what I do in a usual week.
I can say what I'm doing this week, when it is different.
I can say what I have to do and what I don't have to do.
I can read a job advert and part of a contract.
I can ask what a new job needs before I accept it.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first picture. What is the person's job? Do you think it is easy or hard?
reading.talk: Would you like the job in the story? Why, or why not? What do you have to do in your job? Write three sentences, or say them to Wehel.

quiz.q: She ___ wear a uniform. It's a rule.
quiz.why: She takes has to, and a rule means there is no choice.

quiz.q: You ___ bring a laptop. We give you one.
quiz.why: They give you one, so it is not necessary.

quiz.q: Sorry, I can't talk now. I ___ a customer.
The last day to finish a piece of work is the ___ .
quiz.why: A deadline is the last day or time to finish work.

quiz.q: Extra hours after your normal hours are called ___ .
quiz.why: Overtime is extra hours of work.

quiz.q: A job advert says: No experience needed. What does it mean?
options: You need a lot of experience.
quiz.why: Not needed means it is not necessary, so you can apply.

quiz.q: When we say have to fast, the v in have sounds like …
quiz.why: Have to is quick, so the v sounds like f: haf-to.

quiz.q: Go straight on and ___ left at the traffic lights.
quiz.why: Turn left: you go that way.
A question about the past uses did.

quiz.q: I went to the station ___ buy a ticket.
quiz.why: To + a verb says why: to buy a ticket.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the new colleague conversation in pairs. Then change the job: a nurse, a driver, a cook. Listen for a quick have to.
Day 2: a class survey. Learners ask Do you have to wear a uniform? Do you have to work at weekends? Then each learner says what they usually do, and what they're doing this week.
Day 3: the task. Each learner tells a new colleague about their job. Then you are Priya: offer a job, and answer their questions before they accept.
Day 4: talk about the book, answer questions, and let two learners read their job in three parts aloud.
